concepts.name: Rise of the Peshwa: Transition from Chhatrapati to Peshwa Supremacy
key_dimensions: Shift of real power from Chhatrapati to Peshwa under Balaji Vishwanath — constitutional vs. de facto authority
Role of Balaji Vishwanath in consolidating Maratha power post-Aurangzeb — Treaty of Lonavla (1714) context
Distinction between Peshwa as a hereditary office vs. originally a ministerial appointment under Shivaji's Ashtapradhan
UPSC trap: Confusing the first Peshwa (Moropant Trimbak Pingle under Shivaji) with Balaji Vishwanath as the first 'powerful' Peshwa

concepts.name: Balaji Vishwanath's Treaty with the Mughals (1719) — The Sayyid Brothers Alliance
key_dimensions: Terms of the Treaty: Chauth and Sardeshmukhi rights over Deccan, release of Shahu, Maratha recognition of Mughal suzerainty
Role of Sayyid Brothers (Hussain Ali and Abdullah Khan) as kingmakers — Mughal political instability exploited by Marathas
Significance: First formal Mughal recognition of Maratha revenue rights — watershed in Maratha legitimacy
UPSC trap: Distinguishing this treaty's terms from later Treaty of Bhopal (1738) — both involve Mughal-Maratha agreements

concepts.name: Baji Rao I — Military Campaigns and the Concept of 'Hindu Pad Padshahi'
key_dimensions: Ideology of Hindu Pad Padshahi: Maratha suzerainty over all India vs. Mughal suzerainty — political philosophy vs. military reality
Key campaigns: Malwa (1723), Gujarat, Bundelkhand (Mastani episode), and the siege of Delhi (1737)
Battle of Palkhed (1728) against Nizam-ul-Mulk — strategic encirclement tactic, significance as a masterpiece of cavalry warfare
UPSC trap: Confusing Battle of Palkhed (vs. Nizam) with Battle of Bhopal (1738, also vs. Nizam) — different outcomes and treaties

concepts.name: Battle of Palkhed (1728) — Tactical and Strategic Significance
key_dimensions: Context: Nizam-ul-Mulk's attempt to reassert Mughal authority in Deccan vs. Maratha expansion
Baji Rao's strategy of cutting off supply lines rather than direct confrontation — maneuver warfare
Outcome: Treaty of Mungi-Shegaon — Nizam acknowledged Maratha rights to Chauth and Sardeshmukhi
Significance as a turning point: established Maratha dominance in Deccan permanently over the Nizam

concepts.name: Maratha Expansion into Malwa and Gujarat — Administrative and Revenue Dimensions
key_dimensions: Chauth and Sardeshmukhi: Definition, distinction, and how collection rights expanded Maratha territory without direct annexation
Role of Maratha sardars (Holkar, Scindia, Bhonsle, Gaekwad) in governing newly acquired territories — confederacy formation
Tension between central Peshwa authority and autonomous sardars — seeds of later confederacy fragmentation
UPSC trap: Chauth was 1/4th of revenue as protection tax; Sardeshmukhi was an additional 10% — often confused in MCQs

concepts.name: The Maratha Confederacy — Structure, Chiefs, and Relation to Peshwa
key_dimensions: Five major houses: Peshwa (Pune), Bhonsle (Nagpur), Holkar (Indore), Scindia (Gwalior), Gaekwad (Baroda) — territories and founding
Nature of confederacy: loose alliance vs. centralized empire — each chief's autonomy and conflict with Peshwa
UPSC trap: Gaekwad controlled Gujarat but was technically subordinate; Bhonsle of Nagpur was a rival branch of the Bhonsle clan
How confederacy structure contributed to failure at Panipat III — lack of unified command

concepts.name: Baji Rao I's Northern Campaigns — Expansion into Rajputana, Bundelkhand, and Approach to Delhi
key_dimensions: Subjugation of Rajput states: Jaipur, Jodhpur — Maratha extraction of tribute without annexation
Bundelkhand campaign: Alliance with Chhatrasal — Mastani's origin and political alliance dimension
The 1737 raid on Delhi: Symbolic significance of Maratha forces reaching the Mughal capital — psychological blow to Mughal prestige
UPSC trap: Baji Rao never formally captured Delhi; the raid was a demonstration of power, not territorial conquest

concepts.name: Treaty of Bhopal (1738) — Maratha-Mughal Relations and Malwa Cession
key_dimensions: Context: Aftermath of Baji Rao's northern campaigns and Battle of Bhopal against Nizam-backed Mughal forces
Terms: Mughal cession of Malwa to Marathas — significant territorial acquisition legitimized by treaty
Significance: Marked the effective end of Mughal control over central India
Comparison with 1719 Treaty: 1719 gave revenue rights; 1738 gave territorial sovereignty — qualitative leap in Maratha power

concepts.name: Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb) — Administrative Reforms and Peak of Peshwa Power
key_dimensions: Administrative innovations: Revenue reforms, expansion of Pune as a political and cultural center
Territorial expansion: Bengal campaign (Maratha raids into Bengal 1741-1751), Karnataka, and the south
Relationship with Chhatrapati Ramraja — formalization of Peshwa as the de facto ruler, Satara court as ceremonial
UPSC trap: Balaji Baji Rao is often confused with Balaji Vishwanath — different Peshwas, different periods, different achievements

concepts.name: Maratha Raids in Bengal (1741–1751) — The Bargis and Their Impact
key_dimensions: Bargis: Maratha light cavalry used in raids — terrorization of Bengal populace, Bargi raids in Bengali folk memory
Political context: Maratha pressure on Bengal Nawabs (Alivardi Khan) — tribute extraction vs. territorial conquest
Treaty of 1751: Alivardi Khan ceded Orissa and agreed to pay Chauth for Bengal — Maratha reach into eastern India
UPSC trap: Marathas never permanently administered Bengal; these were raids for tribute, not territorial expansion

concepts.name: Maratha-Nizam Rivalry — Recurring Conflicts and Strategic Significance
key_dimensions: Multiple conflicts: Palkhed (1728), Bhopal (1738), Udgir (1760) — each with distinct causes and outcomes
Nizam as a recurring obstacle to Maratha Deccan hegemony and as a sometimes-ally of anti-Maratha forces
Battle of Udgir (1760): Decisive Maratha victory, Nizam ceded large territories including Bidar and Osmanabad areas
UPSC trap: Udgir (1760) is often overshadowed by Panipat III (1761) — but Udgir was a major Maratha triumph just before their greatest defeat

concepts.name: Third Battle of Panipat (1761) — Causes, Course, and Consequences
key_dimensions: Causes: Maratha overextension, alienation of Rajput and Jat allies, Ahmad Shah Abdali's invitation by anti-Maratha coalition including Najib-ud-Daula and Shuja-ud-Daula
Key failure factors: Supply line collapse, Vishwasrao and Viswasrao's deaths, Ibrahim Khan Gardi's artillery advantage negated by Afghan cavalry
Immediate consequences: Death of Viswasrao, Bhausaheb (Vishwasrao Bhau), and the 'emptying of Maharashtra' — demographic and military loss
Long-term consequences: End of Maratha bid for pan-Indian empire, opening for British expansion — UPSC frequently asks on 'who benefited most from Panipat III'

concepts.name: Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani) and the Anti-Maratha Coalition at Panipat
key_dimensions: Composition of coalition: Abdali + Rohilla Afghans (Najib-ud-Daula) + Awadh Nawab (Shuja-ud-Daula) — reasons each joined
Why Rajputs and Jats remained neutral: Maratha failure to build alliances, arrogant treatment of potential allies
Abdali's subsequent withdrawal from India — no permanent Afghan empire established despite victory
UPSC trap: Abdali fought multiple battles in India (Panipat I, II, III are different battles with different combatants — only III involves Abdali)

concepts.name: Madhav Rao I — The Revival of Maratha Power Post-Panipat
key_dimensions: Rapid recovery under Madhav Rao I (1761-1772): Restoration of Maratha influence in Rajputana, re-establishment of control over Nizam and Hyder Ali
Defeat of Hyder Ali (1764, 1767): Maratha reassertion in southern India, limiting Mysore's expansion
Internal challenge: Conflict with Raghunathrao (Raghoba) — uncle's ambitions vs. Peshwa authority, foreshadowing later crisis
UPSC trap: Madhav Rao I is often underrated — his 11-year reign reversed Panipat's damage but his early death at 27 is a key turning point

concepts.name: Raghunathrao (Raghoba) Crisis and the Surat Treaty (1775) — Entry of British into Maratha Affairs
key_dimensions: Raghoba's claim to Peshwaship vs. infant Peshwa Madhavrao II (Sawai Madhavrao) — succession dispute
Treaty of Surat (1775): Raghoba ceded Salsette and Broach to British East India Company in exchange for military support — first formal British-Maratha entanglement
Maratha internal response: Puna Court's repudiation of Surat Treaty, leading to First Anglo-Maratha War
UPSC trap: Treaty of Surat (1775) is different from Treaty of Salbai (1782) — Surat started the war, Salbai ended the First Anglo-Maratha War

concepts.name: First Anglo-Maratha War (1775–1782) and Treaty of Salbai
key_dimensions: Key engagements: Battle of Wadgaon (1779) — rare British defeat, Convention of Wadgaon (humiliating British withdrawal)
British strategic response: Warren Hastings' coordinated attacks from multiple fronts (Bengal, Bombay, Madras)
Treaty of Salbai (1782): Status quo ante bellum — British retained Salsette, Marathas got back Raghoba's cessions; 20-year peace clause
Significance: Demonstrated Maratha military resilience but also revealed confederacy's inability to deliver a knockout blow

concepts.name: Nana Fadnavis — Diplomacy, Political Management, and the 'Maratha Metternich'
key_dimensions: Role as regent/minister under successive weak Peshwas — managing confederacy politics without military command
Diplomatic maneuvers: Playing British, Nizam, Hyder Ali/Tipu Sultan against each other to preserve Maratha independence
Formation of the Triple Alliance (Marathas, Hyderabad, Mysore) against British — why it failed to materialize effectively
UPSC trap: Nana Fadnavis is often called 'the last of the Marathas' — his death in 1800 directly preceded British victory in Second Anglo-Maratha War

concepts.name: Maratha Revenue System — Chauth, Sardeshmukhi, and Mokasa
key_dimensions: Chauth: 1/4th of revenue as protection tax paid to Marathas by non-Maratha territories — not direct administration
Sardeshmukhi: Additional 10% claimed by Peshwa as hereditary right over Deccan — distinction from Chauth
Mokasa/Jagir system within Maratha territory: Assignment of revenue to sardars — how it created autonomous power centers
UPSC trap: Chauth and Sardeshmukhi were originally Shivaji's innovations but were massively expanded in territorial scope during Peshwa period

concepts.name: Maratha Expansion in the South — Karnataka, Mysore, and the Tamil Country
key_dimensions: Maratha campaigns in Karnataka under Balaji Baji Rao and Madhav Rao I — conflict with Hyder Ali over the region
Battle of Rakshasbhuvan (1763): Maratha victory over Nizam in Marathwada — consolidation before southern campaigns
Madhav Rao I's multiple campaigns against Hyder Ali — strategic importance of Sira and Mysore borderlands
UPSC trap: Marathas were the first major challengers to Hyder Ali's expansion, not the British — often overlooked in favor of Anglo-Mysore Wars narrative

concepts.name: Peshwa Madhavrao II (Sawai Madhavrao) and the Twilight of the Peshwa Period
key_dimensions: Reign under regency of Nana Fadnavis — nominal vs. real authority, parallel to earlier Chhatrapati-Peshwa dynamic
Continued Maratha influence despite internal strife: Last phase of Maratha military campaigns in north India
His death (suicide, 1795) triggering the final succession crisis — Raghoba's son Baji Rao II becoming Peshwa
UPSC trap: Sawai Madhavrao's death is the functional end of effective Peshwa governance — Baji Rao II's Peshwaship belongs to decline/Anglo-Maratha Wars phase
